group.title: More phrasal verbs
group.tagline: Set off, turn down, put up with
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: To start a journey.
examples: We {set off} early to avoid the traffic.
wrong: We set off at six and stayed at home all day.

words.meaning: To accept something unpleasant without complaining.
examples: I can’t {put up with} this noise any longer.
wrong: She couldn’t put up with the noise, so she said nothing and stayed.

words.meaning: To try to find out the facts about something.
examples: The manager will {look into} your complaint.
wrong: The police looked into the crime by ignoring it completely.

words.meaning: To think of an idea, plan or answer.
examples: She {came up with} a clever plan.
wrong: He came up with a great idea, but he had no idea at all.

words.meaning: To meet someone you know by chance.
examples: I {ran into} my old teacher at the supermarket.
wrong: I ran into my friend, as we had planned for weeks.

words.meaning: To throw away or remove something you don’t want.
examples: I need to {get rid of} these old clothes.
wrong: We got rid of the old sofa and kept it in the living room.

words.meaning: To finally agree to something after saying no for a long time.
examples: My parents {gave in} and let me get a dog.
wrong: He gave in and kept saying no until the very end.

words.meaning: To give something to someone without asking for money.
examples: He {gave away} all his books to the library.
wrong: She gave away her bike and asked for fifty dollars.

words.meaning: To do a task, plan or test.
examples: The scientists {carried out} an experiment.
wrong: They carried out the plan by never starting it.

words.meaning: To finally be in a place or situation you didn’t plan.
examples: We got lost and {ended up} in the next town.
wrong: We ended up at the start of the trip, before we left.

words.meaning: To experience something difficult.
examples: She {went through} a hard time after the accident.
wrong: He went through a hard year in which everything was easy.

words.meaning: To think you are better than someone.
examples: Don’t {look down on} people with less money.
wrong: She looks down on her neighbors because she admires them so much.

words.meaning: To stop a fire or light from burning.
examples: Firefighters {put out} the fire in ten minutes.
wrong: He put out the candle so it would burn brighter.

words.meaning: To use or do less of something.
examples: I’m trying to {cut down on} sugar.
wrong: He cut down on coffee by drinking twice as much.

words.meaning: To move or learn as fast as others.
examples: I walk fast, so she can’t {keep up with} me.
wrong: She kept up with the other runners and finished far behind.

words.meaning: To disappoint someone by not doing what they hoped.
examples: I felt {let down} when he didn’t come to my party.
wrong: He let down his team by scoring the winning goal.

words.meaning: To leave a place quickly and secretly to escape.
examples: The dog {ran away} when the gate was open.
wrong: The cat ran away and stayed in the garden all day.

words.meaning: To give back money you borrowed.
examples: I’ll {pay back} the money next week.
wrong: She paid back the loan by borrowing more and never returning it.

words.meaning: To start a calm life in one place, often with a family.
examples: After years of travel, they {settled down} in a small town.
wrong: He settled down and moved to a new country every month.

words.meaning: To take control of something from someone else.
examples: A new manager will {take over} the team in May.
wrong: She took over the company and gave up all control.

words.meaning: To happen or end in a certain way, often a surprise.
examples: The test {turned out} to be easy.
wrong: The party turned out well before it had even started.

words.meaning: To use something until it is old and can’t be used.
examples: I {wore out} my shoes in three months.
wrong: These strong new boots will wear out after just one short walk, so they will last for years.

words.meaning: To reach someone ahead of you, or the level of others.
examples: Go ahead, I’ll {catch up} with you later.
wrong: I caught up with the bus by staying far behind it.

words.meaning: To put your name on a list to join something.
examples: I {signed up} for a yoga class.
wrong: He signed up for the club and never became a member.

words.meaning: To be easy to see or notice because it is different.
examples: Her red coat {stands out} in the crowd.
wrong: His bright orange suit stood out, so no one noticed him.

words.meaning: To leave a school, course or race before the end.
examples: He {dropped out} of college after a year.
wrong: She dropped out of the race and finished it first.

words.meaning: To break into pieces because it is old or badly made.
examples: My old bag is {falling apart}.
wrong: The cheap chair fell apart, so it is as strong as ever.

words.meaning: To feel accepted as part of a group.
examples: It took time to {fit in} at my new school.
wrong: He fit in well, so he always felt like an outsider.

words.meaning: To do something wrong and not be punished.
examples: He cheated and {got away with} it.
wrong: She got away with the crime and spent ten years in prison.

words.meaning: To start or continue doing something, often after permission.
examples: If you want to ask a question, {go ahead}.
wrong: The concert went ahead, so it was canceled.

words.meaning: To make someone or something late.
examples: Sorry I’m late, I was {held up} in traffic.
wrong: The traffic held us up, so we arrived early.

words.meaning: To think one person or thing is another by mistake.
examples: People often {mix up} the twins.
wrong: I mixed up their names because I knew them perfectly.

words.meaning: To stop thinking about something and start something new.
examples: It’s time to {move on} to the next topic.
wrong: She moved on and kept thinking only about the past.

words.meaning: To try to make people admire you or your things.
examples: He’s always {showing off} his new car.
wrong: She showed off her new phone by hiding it from everyone.

words.meaning: To not go to bed until later than usual.
examples: We {stayed up} late to watch the film.
wrong: I stayed up all night, so I went to bed at eight.

words.meaning: To accept a job, duty or new worker.
examples: I can’t {take on} any more work this week.
wrong: He took on the project and refused to do it.

words.meaning: To think carefully about something before you decide.
examples: Let me {think over} your offer.
wrong: She thought over the offer by deciding in one second.

words.meaning: To give something to each person in a group.
examples: The teacher {handed out} the tests.
wrong: He handed out the leaflets and kept them all himself.

words.meaning: To trust someone to help you.
examples: You can always {count on} me.
wrong: I counted on him, so I never trusted him with anything.

words.meaning: To have just enough money or skill to live or manage.
examples: We {get by} on a small income.
wrong: They get by easily with millions to spare.
